sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** Retry mechanisms re-attempt a failed operation (network call, message processing, DB write) with a controlled delay strategy — typically exponential backoff with jitter — bounded by a maximum number of attempts, a retry budget, and integration with a circuit breaker to prevent cascading failures.

Retries are the simplest resilience primitive in distributed systems and also the most dangerous. When a downstream service experiences a brief failure (a 503 for two seconds, a connection timeout, a transient DNS hiccup), the right reaction is to wait briefly and try again — most transient failures resolve within milliseconds to seconds, and a single retry turns a user-visible failure into a silent success. The wrong reaction is to retry aggressively in a tight loop, which amplifies load on the already-struggling downstream: 1,000 callers each retrying every 10ms add 100,000 extra requests per second to a service that is already failing, accelerating its collapse. This dynamic — retries turning a minor degradation into a catastrophic outage — is so common it has a name: retry storms. The 2015 AWS DynamoDB outage, the 2019 Cloudflare outage, and numerous Google SRE postmortems all cite retry amplification as a contributing factor. The discipline of doing retries correctly is therefore not optional: every production caller must use exponential backoff, jitter, a bounded max-attempts, and ideally a retry budget.

Exponential backoff is the foundational strategy. Instead of retrying at a fixed interval (e.g., every 100ms), the caller waits an interval that doubles after each failure: 100ms, 200ms, 400ms, 800ms, 1600ms, capping at some maximum (e.g., 30 seconds). This gives the downstream time to recover: if the failure is a brief overload, the reduced request rate helps; if it is a deployment rolling restart, the increasing gaps span the restart window; if it is a network partition, the longer waits reduce pointless traffic. The doubling continues until either the operation succeeds, the max-attempts limit (typically 3–5 for synchronous calls, 10+ for asynchronous background workers) is reached, or the cap is hit. AWS SDKs default to exponential backoff with a 1-second cap for DynamoDB, the gRPC retry policy supports `exponential backoff` with configurable initial/final/max-attempts, and the Google Cloud client libraries use a 1s+random-jitter initial backoff doubling to a 60s cap. The pattern is universal: every mature client library implements it, and every architect should ensure it is enabled, not disabled.

Pure exponential backoff has a subtle flaw: synchronized retries. If 1,000 clients all fail at the same moment (a partition heals, a deployment lands, a cache flushes) and all use the same backoff schedule (100ms, 200ms, 400ms), they will all retry at the same instants, producing a thundering herd of synchronized waves that re-overloads the downstream. The fix is jitter — adding random noise to each retry interval so clients desynchronize. Two common jitter strategies exist: "full jitter" picks a uniformly random value between 0 and the exponential backoff (e.g., for a 400ms backoff, pick uniform in [0, 400ms]); "equal jitter" splits the backoff in half and randomizes the second half (e.g., 200ms + uniform[0, 200ms]). AWS recommends full jitter in its architecture blog post on exponential backoff, and the AWS SDK uses it by default. The visual difference is striking: without jitter, retry traffic arrives in spikes; with jitter, it spreads into a smooth, lower-amplitude wave that the downstream can absorb. Jitter is essentially free (one call to a random number generator) and provides enormous resilience benefit — there is no excuse for omitting it.

Max attempts and retry budgets bound the total retry effort. Max attempts is the simple cap: "retry at most 3 times, then give up and surface the error to the caller." This prevents a single failed request from consuming a connection for minutes. A retry budget is a more sophisticated limit: it caps the fraction of total requests that can be retries, rather than the retries per request. For example, if the budget is 10% and the current request rate is 1,000/s with 100 retries/s, retries are allowed; if retries climb to 200/s (20% of total), new retries are rejected (the caller gets the failure immediately instead of retrying). This prevents a downstream outage from causing the caller to spend most of its capacity on retries — when 50% of requests are failing, allowing 3 retries per request triples the effective load, and a budget stops this. The gRPC retry budget, Envoy's retry budgets, and the Google SRE "retry budget" pattern (10% of requests, with a TTL of 10 seconds) all implement this idea. Netflix Hystrix implemented a similar concept via its circuit breaker: when the failure rate exceeded a threshold (default 50%), the circuit opened and all requests failed fast without retrying, giving the downstream time to recover.

Circuit breaker integration is the final layer. A circuit breaker tracks the recent failure rate of a downstream and, when it exceeds a threshold, "opens" — meaning all subsequent calls fail immediately without even attempting the network round-trip. This protects the downstream from any traffic at all (including retries) and forces the caller to surface the failure to the user immediately. After a cooldown period (e.g., 10 seconds), the circuit enters "half-open" state: a small number of test requests are allowed through; if they succeed, the circuit closes and full traffic resumes; if they fail, the circuit re-opens for another cooldown. Hystrix popularized this pattern; Resilience4j is its modern successor; gRPC has circuit breakers built into Envoy; and AWS's "circuit breaker" on Application Load Balancers protects against unhealthy targets. The interaction between retry and circuit breaker is critical: retry handles individual request failures (transient, isolated), while circuit breaker handles systemic downstream failures (sustained, correlated). Without a circuit breaker, retry can amplify an outage; without retry, transient failures become user-visible. The architect's rule: use both — retry with exponential backoff + jitter for transient failures, circuit breaker for sustained failures, and ensure the retry logic checks the circuit state before retrying (if the circuit is open, do not retry; surface the failure immediately).

sections.title: Visual Explanation
sections.body:
### Mermaid Diagram
```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant S as Downstream Service
    participant CB as Circuit Breaker
    C->>S: Request attempt 1
    S-->>C: 503 (transient)
    Note over C: backoff = 100ms + jitter(0-100ms)
    C->>C: sleep(150ms)
    C->>S: Request attempt 2
    S-->>C: 503 (transient)
    Note over C: backoff = 200ms + jitter(0-200ms)
    C->>C: sleep(310ms)
    C->>S: Request attempt 3
    S-->>C: 503 (transient)
    Note over CB: failure rate > 50% -> OPEN
    C->>CB: Request attempt 4
    CB-->>C: fail-fast (circuit open, no retry)
    Note over C: surface error to caller
```

### ASCII Diagram
```
   +--------+        attempt 1 (fail)         +-----------+
   |        |--------------------------------->|           |
   |        |<------- 503 -------------------|           |
   |        |                                  | Downstream|
   |        |  sleep(100ms + jitter)           |  Service  |
   |        |  attempt 2 (fail)                |           |
   | Client |--------------------------------->|           |
   |        |<------- 503 -------------------|           |
   |        |                                  |           |
   |        |  sleep(200ms + jitter)           |           |
   |        |  attempt 3 (fail)                |           |
   |        |--------------------------------->|           |
   |        |<------- 503 -------------------|           |
   |        |                                  +-----------+
   |        |  attempt 4: check circuit
   |        |--+        +---------------------+
   |        |   |       |  Circuit Breaker    |
   |        |<--+       |  OPEN (fail fast)   |
   |        |           +---------------------+
   |        |  -> surface error to caller
   +--------+
```

### Walkthrough
1. The client sends the request and receives a 503 (transient failure). It computes the backoff as `base * 2^(attempt-1)` and adds a random jitter to desynchronize from other clients, then sleeps before retrying.
2. After multiple failures, the circuit breaker (tracking the downstream's failure rate) opens — subsequent calls fail fast without a network round-trip, protecting the downstream from further load.
3. The client checks the circuit state before retrying: if open, it does not retry and instead surfaces the error to the caller. After a cooldown, the circuit half-opens to test recovery.

quiz.explanation: A retry storm is a positive-feedback loop where retries amplify load on a failing downstream, accelerating its collapse. It typically unfolds as: downstream degrades briefly, callers begin retrying, the retry traffic pushes the downstream further into overload, more requests fail, more retries happen, the downstream crashes or becomes unresponsive, and the cascade spreads to upstream callers who also begin retrying.
